title: Leadership Lessons From Building a 45-Person Mortgage Team
description: What I've learned growing from branch manager to leading a team of 45 loan officers and staff, and the leadership habits that matter most in mortgage.
image_alt: Three men seated in chairs talking in a modern office

faq.q: What makes a good mortgage team leader?
faq.a: Accessibility, honesty, consistent coaching, and a genuine investment in each person's growth, along with a deep understanding of the business.

faq.q: How do you keep a mortgage team motivated in tough markets?
faq.a: Focus the team on what it controls, celebrate effort and wins, share knowledge openly, and keep leadership visible and accessible.

faq.q: Should mortgage leaders still originate loans?
faq.a: Many effective leaders stay close to production in some form, because it keeps them credible and connected to what their team experiences every day.

body_html:
When I became a branch manager, I thought leadership meant having the answers. Leading a team that grew to 45 loan officers and support staff taught me something different: leadership is mostly about creating the conditions for other people to do their best work. Here are the lessons that have mattered most.

1. Be accessible, especially when it's inconvenient

The fastest way to lose a team is to become unreachable. Loan officers deal with time-sensitive problems: a condition that could blow a closing, an agent who needs an answer tonight, a client who's panicking. When a leader picks up the phone, the whole team moves faster and with more confidence. Accessibility isn't a perk; it's the job.

2. Focus the team on what it controls

Markets change. Rates move. Headlines get loud. A team that spends its energy reacting to things it can't control burns out. I try to keep our focus on what we can control: conversations, follow-up, service, relationships, and learning. In good markets and tough ones, that focus is what separates teams that grow from teams that stall.

Nobody wins by watching the 10-year all day. You win by doing the work in front of you better than anyone else.

3. Coach the person, not just the pipeline

Pipeline reports matter, but people aren't spreadsheets. Some loan officers need help with confidence. Some need structure. Some need to learn to say no to the wrong deals. Regular one-on-one time, focused on the individual's goals, does more for production than any contest.

4. Make knowledge flow freely

On a strong team, scenarios get shared, wins get explained, and mistakes become lessons instead of secrets. When a loan officer figures out how to close a tough bank statement loan or a tricky condo, the whole team should benefit. Creating that culture takes intention: team calls, open channels, and leaders who share their own lessons first.

5. Hire for character and coachability

Skills can be taught. Integrity, work ethic, and a willingness to learn are much harder to coach. I've written more about this in what I look for when hiring loan officers. The best hires I've made weren't always the most experienced; they were the most committed.

6. Celebrate the right things

CelebrateWhy
Great client reviewsService is the foundation of referrals
Problem files that closedShows creativity and persistence
New agent partnershipsBuilds long-term pipeline
Teammates helping teammatesReinforces the culture you want
Personal milestonesPeople are more than their production

7. Protect integrity without exception

Mortgage lending is regulated for good reasons. A leader sets the tone on compliance and honesty. That means never rewarding shortcuts, addressing issues quickly, and making it safe for people to raise concerns. A team's reputation takes years to build and one bad decision to damage.

8. Keep learning yourself

Serving on United Wholesale Mortgage's Advisory Council has reminded me how much there is to learn from other leaders and brokers across the country. The leaders I admire most are curious. They ask questions, listen to their teams, and keep improving.

9. Think in years, not months

Short-term thinking leads to short-term teams. Investing in people, culture, and systems pays off slowly, then all at once. The goal isn't one great month. It's building something that lasts.

What I'd tell a new branch manager

If I could give one piece of advice to someone stepping into leadership for the first time, it would be this: your job changed, even if your title is the only thing that looks different. Your success is now measured by the success of the people around you. That means spending more time listening than talking, more time coaching than closing, and more time thinking about the next two years than the next two weeks.

10. Make the mission bigger than any one month

Teams rally around a shared purpose. For us, that's helping families get into homes and helping loan officers build careers they're proud of. When the mission is clear, the hard days make more sense, and the wins mean more. Leaders have to say the mission out loud, often, and then prove it through how they make decisions.

That's also why I believe in setting ambitious goals in public. A clear target gives a team something to build toward together, and it creates accountability for leaders as much as anyone. The goal isn't to pressure people; it's to show them where we're going and invite them to help build it.

The takeaway

Leadership in mortgage comes down to being present, focusing on what you control, investing in people, and protecting integrity. Those principles helped me build a team I'm proud of, and they're what I'm bringing to the next chapter. If you're a loan officer looking for that kind of leadership, let's talk.
